Multiple small periventricular and subcortical T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensities without restricted diffusion or enhancement; imaging differential includes small vessel ischemia or inflammatory change. 2. Subtle bilateral thalamic FLAIR signal with minimal diffusion restriction, consistent with peri-ictal change. 3. No infarct, vasogenic edema, hemorrhage, mass or abnormal enhancement. The pattern is nonspecific; clinical correlation recommended.

output.interpretation: Neural antibody panel (serum) negative. A negative result does not exclude autoimmune encephalitis. Clinical correlation recommended.

contraindications: Phenytoin, fosphenytoin, oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine: documented carbamazepine Stevens-Johnson syndrome; cross-reactive severe cutaneous reactions among aromatic ASMs; avoid.
Valproate with hyperammonemia (ammonia 84 umol/L): valproate-associated hyperammonemic encephalopathy; do not reload or continue.
interactions: Fosphenytoin or phenytoin + prednisone: CYP3A4 induction lowers prednisolone exposure.
Levetiracetam + prednisone or hydroxychloroquine: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; maintenance dose by creatinine clearance (creatinine 1.4).
Lacosamide + current medications: no relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; lacosamide prolongs the PR interval.
Valproate + carbapenems (for example meropenem): carbapenems lower valproate levels sharply within a day.
Lorazepam + current medications: no relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; additive respiratory depression with other sedatives.
output.proposed: Lorazepam, a second-line antiseizure medication (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate or lacosamide) and L-carnitine with valproic acid, hydroxychloroquine and prednisone
warnings: Hydroxychloroquine can lower the seizure threshold and prolong the QT interval (labelled warnings).
Valproate: major teratogen; avoid in women of childbearing potential when an alternative exists.

results.finding: Valproate-associated hyperammonemia can occur with levels in or below the therapeutic range and presents with encephalopathy and increased seizures.
Management is withdrawal of valproate and IV L-carnitine, typically a 100 mg/kg loading dose (maximum 6 g) followed by 15 mg/kg every 4 hours.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive status epilepticus.

output.summary: Valproate-associated hyperammonemia can occur at any valproate level and is managed by withdrawing valproate and giving IV L-carnitine [Lheureux_2009]. Of the second-line agents for status epilepticus, levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate were equally effective in ESETT [ESETT_2019].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproate 36 mcg/mL (low) with ammonia 84 umol/L (high); creatinine 1.4; lactate 8.8 with pH 7.15 after the convulsion; anemia 10.2, platelets 124, dsDNA 142 with low C3 and C4 and proteinuria (active SLE); procalcitonin normal, no pyuria; beta-hCG negative
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, valproate level, ammonia, beta-hCG
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of seizures and decide the ASM and its dose; the valproate level tests adherence, ammonia detects valproate-associated hyperammonemia, and a pregnancy test in a woman of reproductive age changes ASM choice [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Two sets drawn before antimicrobials: no growth to date
action_criteria.label: Two sets of blood cultures: fever since yesterday on prednisone 40 mg
action_criteria.rationale: Fever that began before the seizure in a patient on prednisone keeps bacteremia open; cultures are drawn before any antimicrobial [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute abnormality; subtle nonspecific periventricular white matter hypodensities
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT after stabilization
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes hemorrhage, mass or edema that would change management, and must precede any LP [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Continuous generalized 2-4 Hz polyspike-and-wave, bifrontal maximal, evolving and time-locked to the convulsions
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to confirm ongoing seizures and monitor treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Convulsive SE over 25 minutes needs EEG confirmation of seizure control, since convulsive SE may continue as non-convulsive SE, and hyperammonemia also impairs consciousness; continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours [Brophy_2012]; terminology [ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Nonspecific white matter hyperintensities without restriction or enhancement and peri-ictal thalamic signal; no infarct, PRES pattern or cerebritis
action_criteria.label: MRI brain to characterize the white matter changes and exclude neuropsychiatric lupus, PRES or infarct
action_criteria.rationale: Active SLE on steroids with hypertension and nephritis carries structural causes of SE (PRES, antiphospholipid infarct, cerebritis) that CT can miss; MRI is indicated when autoimmune disease is suspected [Brophy_2012; Fugate_2015].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis 12/uL with protein 58, normal glucose ratio; Gram stain, culture and HSV PCR negative; NMDAR antibodies negative
action_criteria.label: Lumbar puncture after CT: exclude CNS infection in a febrile immunosuppressed patient, and neuropsychiatric lupus
action_criteria.rationale: Fever that began before the seizure in a patient on prednisone 40 mg makes CNS infection a must-exclude; CSF also screens for inflammatory or autoimmune causes; CT first, platelets 124 and INR 1.0 permit LP [Tunkel_2008; Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum neural antibody panel negative (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, AMPAR, GABA-B, GAD65)
action_criteria.label: Serum autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel (SLE with seizures)
action_criteria.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is a treatable cause of SE in a patient with systemic autoimmunity; a serum panel complements the CSF [Graus_2016].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Aromatic ASMs (phenytoin, fosphenytoin, oxcarbazepine) excluded by carbamazepine SJS; valproate excluded by hyperammonemia; phenytoin lowers prednisolone exposure; levetiracetam without relevant interaction, dosed for renal function
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction check for the second-line ASM: carbamazepine SJS, hyperammonemia on valproate, prednisone
action_criteria.rationale: Her carbamazepine SJS excludes the aromatic ASMs and the hyperammonemia excludes valproate, which leaves the choice among the remaining second-line drugs to this check [ESETT_2019; Lheureux_2009].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on valproate withdrawal and L-carnitine for valproate-associated hyperammonemia
action_criteria.label: Literature: valproate-associated hyperammonemic encephalopathy
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step of the work-up.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not reload or continue valproate: ammonia is 84 umol/L, and valproate-associated hyperammonemia is managed by withdrawing it [Lheureux_2009].
Do not give phenytoin, fosphenytoin, oxcarbazepine or carbamazepine: documented carbamazepine Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Do not start cyclophosphamide or pulse methylprednisolone for presumed CNS lupus: MRI and CSF do not show neuropsychiatric lupus.
Do not delay seizure control while the autoimmune work-up is pending.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid valproate because of the hyperammonemia and fosphenytoin because of her carbamazepine Stevens-Johnson syndrome (cross-reactivity among aromatic ASMs) [ESETT_2019].
Stop valproate and give IV L-carnitine (100 mg/kg loading dose, maximum 6 g, then 15 mg/kg every 4 hours), rechecking ammonia [Lheureux_2009].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
If seizures continue after the second-line drug, treat as refractory SE with intubation and a midazolam or propofol infusion under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].
Continue prednisone 40 mg daily (IV equivalent while she cannot swallow) and involve rheumatology for the SLE flare with lupus nephritis; dose levetiracetam maintenance by creatinine clearance.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus from subtherapeutic valproate plus valproate-induced hyperammonemia, in SLE on prednisone

differential.key_features: Ammonia 84 umol/L on valproate (level 36); can occur at any level
Valproate 36 mcg/mL and an uncertain evening dose contribute, but do not explain the hyperammonemia
Ammonia can rise transiently after a generalized convulsion; it may add to the level, but on valproate withdrawal and L-carnitine are indicated regardless
Active SLE (dsDNA 142, low complement), but MRI shows only nonspecific white matter change and CSF a mild nonspecific pleocytosis
CSF NMDAR antibodies and the serum neural antibody panel are negative

differential.diagnosis: CNS infection in an immunosuppressed patient
differential.key_features: Fever on prednisone, but CSF Gram stain, culture, HSV PCR and multiplex PCR negative, blood cultures no growth, procalcitonin normal and no pyuria; the fever accompanies the active SLE flare (ESR 64 with CRP only 9), and the mild lymphocytic pleocytosis is nonspecific after prolonged convulsions in active SLE
SLE, nephritis, steroids and BP 162/98 are risk factors, but MRI shows no vasogenic edema

key_clinical_evidence: Valproate-associated hyperammonemia occurs at any valproate level and is treated by stopping valproate and giving L-carnitine
A carbamazepine Stevens-Johnson syndrome excludes the aromatic ASMs (phenytoin, fosphenytoin, oxcarbazepine) because of cross-reactivity
SLE carries several seizure mechanisms (neuropsychiatric lupus, PRES, antiphospholipid infarct, autoimmune encephalitis, infection on immunosuppression); MRI and CSF exclude them here
Valproate is also avoided in women of reproductive age because of teratogenicity

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The SLE flare is real and needs rheumatology, but MRI and CSF do not show neuropsychiatric lupus; the low valproate level with valproate-associated hyperammonemia explains the SE
red_herrings.data_point: dsDNA 142 IU/mL with low C3 and C4
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests CNS lupus as the primary driver requiring pulse steroids and cyclophosphamide

sequence_constraints.reason: Head CT before LP to exclude mass effect.
The ammonia, valproate level and creatinine decide which second-line ASM is chosen and how it is dosed.

findings.description: Subtle bilateral periventricular white matter hypodensities, nonspecific

ct.impression: 1. No acute intracranial abnormality. No hemorrhage, mass or edema. 2. Subtle bilateral periventricular white matter hypodensities; differential by imaging includes small vessel disease or inflammatory change. MRI recommended for characterization.

eeg.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG. 1. Continuous generalized 2-4 Hz polyspike-and-wave activity, bifrontal maximal, time-locked to bilateral tonic-clonic movements: electrographic status epilepticus. 2. Evolution with frequency decelerating from 3 to 2 Hz. Clinical correlation recommended.
eeg.limitations: Recording begun during convulsive activity; myogenic artifact obscures portions of the record.

labs.interpretation: Leukocytosis (WBC 12.4), anemia (Hb 10.2) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 124). Low bicarbonate (17) with raised anion gap (19) and high lactate (8.8); mixed acidemia on arterial gas (pH 7.15, pCO2 50) with hypoxemia (pO2 60). Creatinine 1.4. Hyperglycemia (214). Low albumin (3.2). Low valproate level (36). High ammonia (84). Mildly raised CK (410). Raised ESR (64) and CRP (9); procalcitonin within range. Raised anti-dsDNA (142) with low C3 (48) and C4 (6). Proteinuria 2+ with microscopic hematuria; leukocyte esterase and nitrite negative. Sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, liver tests and INR within reference ranges. Serum beta-hCG negative.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 6 required actions (labs, CT, continuous EEG, MRI, CSF, drug check) with recommended blood cultures and serum antibody panel and optional literature; GCSE with a low valproate level and valproate-associated hyperammonemia in active SLE on prednisone with fever; teaching points are stopping valproate with L-carnitine, carbamazepine SJS cross-reactivity, excluding infection and neuropsychiatric lupus; 1 grounded red herring.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Davis is a 45-year-old African American woman with generalized epilepsy on valproate and SLE on hydroxychloroquine who is brought by ambulance after her husband found her in the bedroom having a continuous generalized seizure lasting at least 25 minutes. She had taken her morning medications but her husband is not sure about her evening valproate from last night. She has been having an SLE flare over the past 2 weeks with significant joint pain, fatigue, and increased corticosteroid need. Her rheumatologist had started her on prednisone 40 mg daily 10 days ago for the SLE flare. She has had two breakthrough seizures in the past year but no prior SE. Her husband noted she was febrile yesterday with temperature 38.2°C. She has lupus nephritis (class III) with mild proteinuria - baseline creatinine 1.1. She has a documented carbamazepine allergy (severe rash, likely SJS).
